notes: SOURCE: read from the engine own Postgres (hatchet-lite v0.107.0 OLAP tables), not wall-clock in the harness. created_at = v1_tasks_olap.inserted_at (verified byte-identical to the operational v1_task.inserted_at, i.e. the row the engine writes when it creates/queues the task); started_at = max(v1_task_events_olap.event_timestamp) where event_type=STARTED; completed_at = the FINISHED event timestamp. These are exactly the three fields Hatchet own REST API returns as metadata.createdAt / startedAt / finishedAt; one task per run is cross-checked against GET /api/v1/stable/tasks/{id} and agrees within 0.5ms. STARTED/FINISHED are stamped by the worker, which shares the host clock with the engine, so there is no skew. CAVEAT 1 (created_at semantics): Hatchet materialises a DAG lazily - a downstream task row is only inserted once its parent finishes - so created_at for task i>0 is the moment the engine first knew about that task, not a submit time for the whole DAG. It is the closest true queued/scheduled timestamp Hatchet has, but it means created_at tracks the critical path instead of being ~0 for every task. CAVEAT 2 (what one worker means): Hatchet default worker slot count is 100, so one worker process is not one concurrency slot. It does not matter here because the DAG is strictly sequential (task i+1 declares task i as parent) so at most one task is ever runnable; the extractor asserts no two tasks overlap and none did. Python tasks are sync defs, which the SDK runs in a thread pool. CAVEAT 3 (warm-up drift): per-task orchestration latency is not stationary. Under sustained back-to-back load it degraded from ~37 to ~52 ms/task over ~25s, then recovered to ~26-33 ms/task after an idle gap, correlating with Postgres autovacuum on the frequently-updated Dispatcher/Ticker heartbeat tables. The reported reps were therefore taken after a 90s settle, which is the reproducible steady state; a saturated-engine run of the 40-task workload can be ~40 percent slower. CAVEAT 4 (do not use client wall-clock): the SDK result listener appears to resolve on a ~1s grid, so the client-observed wall time was a flat ~2.13s (40x10) and ~4.07s (10x33) regardless of how fast the DAG actually ran; the engine-side timings here are the accurate ones. INTERPRETER: measured with docker exec inside the live worker container, system settled; fibo(33) drifts to ~0.328s if sampled immediately after a benchmark batch. SETUP: one hatchet-lite container (engine+API+gRPC) plus postgres:15.6, and one Python worker process with default settings, all on one m7i.xlarge (4 vCPU, 15GB, Amazon Linux 2023). 1 warmup run discarded, then 5 measured reps.
